bib.title: MIMESIS: Learning User Simulators as Training Environments for Interactive Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MIMESIS: Learning User Simulators as Training Environments for Interactive Agents", Hoang Phan (first author; NYU and Meta Superintelligence Labs, work done at Meta), Changdae Oh, Deren Lei and others. arXiv:2610.09484v2 [cs.AI], dated 8 Oct 2026 on the page-1 stamp. Preprint, no venue. Code: github.com/VietHoang1512/mimesis.
COVERAGE: 40 of 40 pages, all 137,143 chars, including appendices A to G. Extraction was clean except figure text, which is garbled. I skimmed the reference list.

Note on your notes: the paper bears on 06 (data and environments: a simulator is the environment) and 05 (post-training for agents). It touches 07 (reward design) through CSD and the behavior reward. It does not bear on 08 (reasoning RL), apart from the small thinking-supervision ablation below.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Training the agent against MIMESIS-9B beats training against GPT-5.5, under all nine unseen evaluation simulators. Same GRPO, so only the training user changes. Bears on 06.
 number: mean 26.10 to 29.54 (+3.43 per-user mean). Per-user gains run from +1.46 (Claude-Opus-5) to +4.55 (Gemini-3.8-Flash).
 setup: Qwen3-8B agent, UserRL setup, 100 steps. Five training gyms: Travel, TurtleGym, Function, Tau, Persuade. Held out: Intention, Telepathy, Search. Mean score over eight gyms. Single reported number per cell, with no seeds or error bars given for agent results. Training user is MIMESIS-9B or GPT-5.5.
 quote: "raising the mean score from 26.10 to 29.54. Gains range from 1.46 points under Claude-Opus-5 to 4.55 points under Gemini-3.8-Flash." (p.10)
2. CSD (Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation) adds a further gain over GRPO with MIMESIS. Bears on 07.
 number: 29.54 to 31.09 (+1.56). CSD wins on aggregate under all nine users. Mean rank across users: UserRL 3.42, UserRL+ 2.15, CSD 1.75. Exception on rank: Gemini-3.8-Flash, where UserRL+ ranks better than CSD (2.00 vs 2.12).
 setup: as claim 1. CSD settings: alpha=0.01, beta=5.0. The weight is a sigmoid of the gap between teacher and student log-probabilities, applied to the sampled tokens. The coach note is built from the simulator's private thought and next utterance. It is used at training time only. Loss is L_GRPO + alpha*L_CSD.
 quote: "CSD further improves performance under all nine evaluation users, increasing the mean score from 29.54 to 31.09." (p.10)
3. Off-the-shelf frontier LLMs distort task difficulty. A fixed GPT-5.5 agent on tau-bench succeeds 63.6% with real users, but 82.4 to 84.4% with frontier simulators. Pretrained Qwen3.5-4B and 9B give 16.0 and 14.9 points lower. Trained simulators are within 10.3 points; MIMESIS-9B is +2.4 and MIMESIS-4B +1.8. (Fig 2, p.2.) The 63.6% human rate is taken from a prior human study, which I infer; the text does not say.
 quote: "A fixed GPT-5.5 agent succeeds on 63.6% of interactions with real users, whereas the three frontier API simulators raise its success rate to 82.4–84.4%" (p.2)
4. Simulator quality results (Qwen3.5 backbones, 4B and 9B).
 - SOUL-Index: MIMESIS-9B 65.7, Claude-Opus-5 64.9, GPT-5.5 64.1, Osim-8B 58.8, MIMESIS-4B 63.7. Pretrained Qwen3.5-9B is 50.5. Three seeded runs, standard errors reported. The 0.8-point margin over Opus is small. Opus keeps the best ROLE score and GPT-5.5 the best SS score. The CONV gain is large: 75.1 vs 61.7. (Table 1, p.7)
 - RealUserSim Fidelity Index: 94.0 vs 80.6 for Opus. 600 WildChat conversations. (Table 9)
 - SimulatorArena Turing distance: 38.7 vs 42.3 for Opus (lower is better), still far from chance. Opus keeps higher explicit style ratings (3.92 vs 3.70). (Table 11)
 - tau-USI: MIMESIS-9B 80.17, Osim-8B 80.44 (a slight loss), GPT-5.5 76.69, human inter-annotator 91.75. MIMESIS-9B's ECE of 0.069 is the lowest. (Table 10)
 quote: "MIMESIS-9B achieves the highest overall SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing Claude-Opus-5 (64.9), GPT-5.5 (64.1), and the strongest released simulator, Osim-8B (58.8)." (p.7)
5. Ablations (Appendix C).
 - Realistic-behavior training (13 behaviors, ABCD scenarios): RealUserSim 92.3 to 94.0, tau-USI 73.9 to 80.2, SimulatorArena 41.0 to 38.7. This is the largest tau-USI effect. (Fig 12, p.26)
 - Reasoning supervision: on the Mistakes task, response-only SFT collapses accuracy to 25.7. RL recovers it to 36.0 with a median of 1 word of reasoning. ThoughtTrace supervision gives 63.0 with 583 words, against 60.7 for the pretrained model. Flipping the thinking flag at inference does nothing. (Fig 10, p.25)
 - During simulator RL, thinking adds +1.8 (4B) and +1.5 (9B) SOUL points. (Fig 11)
 - User-side mid-training gives more stable RL than starting from the base model, shown only in curves (Fig 9). There is no numeric ablation of the mid-training stage.
6. Baselines for agent training: Base, UserRL (GPT-5.5 user), UserRL+ (MIMESIS user), InfoPO (with the MIMESIS user), CSD. InfoPO was trained with MIMESIS because it "yielded a more robust agent". InfoPO's means are around 24.8 to 28.1, between UserRL and UserRL+ for several users. Example under GPT-5.6: Base 19.42, InfoPO 27.70, UserRL 26.85, UserRL+ 31.10, CSD 32.39. (Tables 15 and 16.) No head-to-head CSD vs InfoPO summary is given. The text says only that CSD "differs operationally" from SDPO and on-policy context distillation.
7. CSD helps with other training simulators. With DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi-K3 as the training user, CSD reaches higher late-stage reward than GRPO (Fig 14, curves only).
8. Theory (Appendix E). Proposition E.1 and Theorem E.2 give a sufficient condition for a GRPO+CSD step to beat a GRPO step: epsilon*S + xi < lambda*||g||. It is a condition on the quality of the coaching weights and is not checked empirically.

QUOTES FOR THE NOTES
- (p.2) "every trained simulator deviates less than every off-the-shelf model, with at most 10.3 points, versus at least 14.9."
- (p.39) "Transfer to human users remains untested, and simulators from different model families may share behavioral biases"
- (p.38 and p.39) "Opus returns stop_reason = "refusal" with no content on all 672 turns". The PersuadeGym reward measures stance change, so every Opus-user cell scores 0.00 and is invalid.

LIMITS (authors concede, plus what I see)
- Human transfer is untested. The nine evaluation users are all LLMs. Of those, GPT-5.6, Claude-Opus-5, Claude-Sonnet-5, Gemini-3.8-Flash and Kimi-K3 are frontier models. Ditto-8B, Osim-8B, HumanLM-8B and Sotopia-7B are released simulators.
- The coaching thoughts are simulator-generated, not human states. Optimizing task reward can reward manipulation, and persuasion is one of the gyms.
- Behavior conditioning can exaggerate traits. MIMESIS-9B over-refuses to authenticate in the retail case (Appendix F.1). A high behavior reward can coexist with constraint violations.
- Mid-training on utterance-only data suppresses reasoning. The authors call their remedy "may discard useful reasoning" and leave better methods to future work.
- Agent results are one reported value per cell (no seeds or confidence intervals) at a small absolute scale. The Persuade column is volatile: for example, under Claude-Sonnet-5 UserRL 38.49, UserRL+ 42.86, CSD 28.17. CSD's gain over UserRL+ is often within a point or two (+0.21 under Gemini, +0.45 under Osim). The 8B agent is the only model size trained.
- The GPT-5.5 baseline is a prompted user; the agent training budget is 100 steps. The paper does not say whether GPT-5.5 was prompted to be non-cooperative, so the comparison is against the default prompt.
- Simulator benchmark gains over the strongest frontier model are small on SOUL (+0.8), and MIMESIS lost to Osim-8B on tau-USI.
- Training-time SOUL scores come from different decode settings than the reported benchmarks.

BUILDS ON: UserRL (Qian et al., 2025: training setup and gyms); GRPO (Shao et al., 2024); ThoughtTrace (Jin et al., 2026: thought supervision and the 13-behavior taxonomy); OdysSim and SOUL (Zhou et al., 2026a); Naous et al. 2025 (user language models); SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026) and On-Policy Context Distillation (Ye et al., 2026) for CSD; Suh et al. 2026 (varying the simulator at fixed training); RealUserSim (Zhu et al., 2026); tau-USI (Zhou et al., 2026b); SimulatorArena (Dou et al., 2025); InfoPO (Kong et al., 2026) as a baseline; ABCD (Chen et al., 2021). The cited model names (GPT-5.5, Claude-Opus-5, Gemini-3.8-Flash and so on) are as printed.

CODE: none. Equations only: CSD weight g = sigmoid(beta * sg(log pi_teacher(y|H,h) - log pi_student(y|H))) (Eq. 8 to 9), and L_agent = L_GRPO + alpha*L_CSD (Eq. 11), p.9. Behavior reward r_beh = (2.0e + 1.5p + 1.0n + 0.5c)/5.0, halved if the simulator describes the behavior instead of expressing it (Eq. 12 to 13, p.17 to 18).

FIGURES: Fig 2 (p.2), the deviation from the real-user success rate per simulator, is the fastest way to see the difficulty-calibration claim. Fig 3 (p.3), the two-stage pipeline overview. Fig 5 (p.9), CSD vs GRPO reward curves. Fig 12 (p.26), the behavior-training ablation. Fig 15 (p.38), a worked example of a coaching note. I did not run the figure captions script.

PROBLEMS: Figure text is garbled in the extraction, so figure values come only from captions and surrounding prose. No embedded instructions found in the PDF. There is a fontTools warning from pypdf that did not affect the text. The paper uses model names that postdate my own knowledge (GPT-5.5, Claude-Opus-5, and others), so I report them as printed and cannot verify them. The tau-bench human success rate of 63.6% is shown only in Fig 2, and the source of that human study is not stated in the pages I read, so check the citation before reusing it.
